title: How to return vector of pointers (and ownership) C++11
body_html:
I have a factory method that creates a bunch of objects and returns pointers to them. Ownership of the objects transfers to the caller:

std::vector<animal*> create_zoo();

This works, but is prone to memory leaks. 

auto zoo = create_zoo();

The vector is on the stack and gets cleaned up automatically, the contained objects are not.

Objects of various sub-types are returned. Returing values instead of pointers won't do.

I was thinking to use

std::vector<std::unique_ptr<animal> > create_zoo();

but unique_ptr don't have copy semantics and I return the vector by value, which, in theory, creates a copy.

I could put the vector on the heap to avoid that

std::unique_ptr<std::vector<std::unique_ptr<animal> > > create_zoo();

but this is getting ridiculous.

This should work too:

std::vector<std::shared_ptr<animal> > create_zoo();

This would work, but it doesn't really transfer ownership. The caller has to assume that there might be other pointers to the objects.

I'm open to suggestions. doesn't need to be std::vector. I'm just looking for a good way of implementing a factory that returns ownership of several objects with modern c++. I'm avoiding boost for now. I'm trying to explore the new c++11 stuff.

events.body_html: std::vector<std::unique_ptr<animal>> will work fine : returning a function-local value will move it, not copy it (or only if moving is not available).

Hmm.. Wouldn't that imply that my code is then dependent on the compiler's ability to perform the "Return Value Optimization"? I understand that all relevant compilers have it implemented, but I'm not sure if they actually guarantee to perform it in all situations. Is this standard practise?

@Stefan no, that's not RVO. RVO would remove the function-local altogether, and use the one on the caller's side in its place. this is about return move-constructing the temmporary returned object (if RVO failed beforehand).
That's the bit I was missing! Returning to c++ after 6 years of Python. I feel both rusty and spoiled. Going to read up on this "move" stuff. thanks!

@Quentin Technically it will (or can) elide the function local, not remove it. (Elision is standard-permitted process of merging object identity in certain (standard-described) cases. All the objects exist, but now their names (if they have them) all refer to the same object with one combined lifetime.)
@Stefan Also, there will be something called "guaranteed copy elision" in C++17 that, I believe, will essentially force RVO-like behavior even without move or copy constructors.

You can also re-consider whether you need the animal objects to be allocated as pointers. std::vector<animal> may also work for your purposes. The animal objects will be allocated with the vector and will move around with it after move operations.
@Yakk thanks for the high-level view. I fell into the trap of explaining the implementation :)
